source: To investigate the sufficiency of the force-detector, we generated chimeric ABDs featuring the H2–H5 bundle region of vinculin and the flexible termini of α-catenin. A vinculin ABD construct where only the CTE was substituted was non-functional (data not shown).
evidence: This is a result from experiments with chimeric constructs.

claim: A vinculin ABD construct featuring both the α-catenin N-terminal segment and the CTE (vinc ABD-NCSwap) gained force-activated binding activity, with diminished low-force binding observed.
source: However, consistent with structural coordination between the α-catenin N-terminal segment and the CTE through the tryptophan latch (Figure 5C; Figure 5—video 1), a construct featuring both the α-catenin N-terminal segment and the CTE (vinc ABD-NCSwap, Materials and methods) gained force-activated binding activity, with diminished low-force binding observed (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; Figure 6—video 2) in contrast to the wild-type vinculin ABD (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a result from TIRF experiments with a chimeric construct.

claim: A C-terminal truncation of vinc ABD-NCSwap (vinc ABD-NCSwapΔC) equivalent to α-cat ABDΔC reverted to constitutive binding regardless of force.
source: A C-terminal truncation of this construct (vinc ABD-NCSwapΔC) equivalent to α-cat ABDΔC reverted to constitutive binding regardless of force (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C; Figure 6—video 3)

claim: The α-catenin CTE is the key determinant of force-activated binding, in which residues 872–906 serve as the force-detector.

claim: The distal C-terminus (residues 872–906) of α-catenin is necessary and sufficient for force-activated actin binding through negative regulation of low-force binding.
source: We thus conclude that the distal C-terminus (residues 872–906) of α-catenin is necessary and sufficient for force-activated actin binding through negative regulation of low-force binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on truncation and chimeric constructs.

claim: α-catenin preferentially binds tensed F-actin, using its flexible C-terminus to detect piconewton load that can be generated by myosin motors.
source: Our studies reveal that α-catenin preferentially binds tensed F-actin, using its flexible C-terminus to detect piconewton load that can be generated by myosin motors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Force-activated F-actin binding could play an important role in the formation and reinforcement of cell-cell adhesion complexes, facilitating mechanically regulated interactions between α-catenin and actomyosin cables tuned for high sensitivity to motor-generated forces.
source: We propose this force-activated F-actin binding could play an important role in the formation and reinforcement of cell-cell adhesion complexes, facilitating mechanically regulated interactions between α-catenin and actomyosin cables tuned for high sensitivity to motor-generated forces.

claim: Actin filaments are themselves tension sensors that can transduce mechanical force into regulated partner binding.
source: We further provide evidence that actin filaments are themselves tension sensors that can transduce mechanical force into regulated partner binding.
evidence: This is a general conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The force-detector element of α-catenin can be functionally transplanted to vinculin, demonstrating that force-activated F-actin binding is a modular activity that can be conferred by short sequence motifs.
source: Our finding that the force-detector element of α-catenin can be functionally transplanted to vinculin demonstrates that force-activated F-actin binding is a modular activity that can be conferred by short sequence motifs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chimeric construct experiments.

claim: There may be other actin-binding proteins with functionally analogous force-detectors, which could broadly mediate mechanotransduction through the cytoskeleton.
source: We thus speculate there may be other actin-binding proteins with functionally analogous force-detectors, which could broadly mediate mechanotransduction through the cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a speculation about broader implications of the findings.

claim: The exact molecular mechanism by which the final 35 amino acids of α-catenin negatively regulate low-force binding to F-actin remains to be elucidated.
source: While our studies pinpoint the final 35 amino acids of α-catenin as a force-detector, the exact molecular mechanism by which this segment negatively regulates low-force binding to F-actin remains to be elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge and future research needs.

claim: One potential model for force-activated binding invokes steric exclusion, where the force-detector physically blocks the adjacent binding site through steric hindrance in the absence of force, which can be relieved by an increase in protomer axial spacing in the presence of tension.
source: As we observe the distal tip of the ordered region of the CTE to be in close apposition to the next ABD binding site along the actin filament, with potential contacts between CTE residues V870 and K871 with the H4–H5 loop and the N-terminal tip of H5 in longitudinally adjacent ABD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), the first model invokes steric exclusion (Figure 7A). In the absence of force, the force-detector (Figure 6; Figure 7) physically blocks the adjacent binding site through steric hindrance, which can be relieved by an increase in protomer axial spacing in the presence of tension
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic model based on structural observations.

claim: Residues 884–906 of α-catenin may inhibit α-catenin's actin binding.
source: consistent with prior truncation studies suggesting residues 884–906 may inhibit α-catenin's actin binding (Pappas and Rimm, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the steric exclusion model, tension-dependent increase of the binding on-rate at the adjacent site would occur due to its increased fractional availability in the presence of thermal fluctuations.
source: As the force-detector likely represents a flexibly tethered conformational ensemble, in the presence of thermal fluctuations we envision this would manifest as a tension-dependent increase of the binding on-rate at the site due to its increased fractional availability.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism within the steric exclusion model.

claim: Cooperative F-actin binding by the α-catenin ABD has previously been reported under non-saturating conditions.
source: Although saturating the filament for structural studies could lead to non-physiological inter-ABD interactions, cooperative F-actin binding by the α-catenin ABD has previously been reported under non-saturating conditions (Hansen et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Supplemental soluble ABD enhanced catch-bonding by the cadherin complex.
source: and supplemental soluble ABD enhanced catch-bonding by the cadherin complex (Buckley et al., 2014)

source: suggesting communication between actin-bound ABDs is likely to be physiologically relevant.

claim: Cooperative and inhibitory inter-ABD communication are not a priori mutually exclusive, and the interplay of these opposing effects could produce differential outcomes as a function of ABD concentration and filament load.
source: We note that cooperative and inhibitory inter-ABD communication are not a priori mutually exclusive, and the interplay of these opposing effects could produce differential outcomes as a function of ABD concentration and filament load, an important subject for future studies.
evidence: This is a speculation about the complexity of the mechanism.

claim: A second potential model for force-activated binding invokes a conformational change in the actin protomer that specifically occurs in the presence of mechanical load, which is recognized and preferentially bound by the force-detector, relieving inhibition.
source: The second model invokes a conformational change in the actin protomer that specifically occurs in the presence of mechanical load, which is recognized and preferentially bound by the force-detector, relieving inhibition (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic model.

claim: The structural studies do not rule out as yet unobserved actin conformations specifically evoked by force.
source: Although our studies suggest only minor actin conformational changes when the binding is driven by mass action (Figure 5H), they do not rule out as yet unobserved actin conformations specifically evoked by force.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current structural data.

claim: Low piconewton forces could modulate the intrinsic structural fluctuations of F-actin to control α-catenin engagement through either steric exclusion or conformational change mechanisms.
source: Furthermore, while for simplicity we have framed both models in terms of discrete transitions between structural states, low piconewton forces could also modulate the intrinsic structural fluctuations of F-actin to control α-catenin engagement through either mechanism, as has previously been speculated for cofilin (Galkin et al., 2012; Hayakawa et al., 2011; Wioland et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism, supported by citations to prior work on cofilin.

claim: Structural studies of the α-catenin ABD–F-actin interface in the presence of active force generation, as well as supporting functional experiments, will be necessary to dissect the interplay of the proposed mechanistic models.
source: Although currently technically prohibitive, structural studies of the α-catenin ABD–F-actin interface in the presence of active force generation, as well as supporting functional experiments, will be necessary to dissect the interplay of these models.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Approximately 1 pN of tension along individual filaments is sufficient for force-activated binding, suggesting that the actin-binding interface of α-catenin has been evolutionarily optimized to sense contractile forces generated by myosin motors.
source: Our finding that approximately 1 pN of tension along individual filaments is sufficient for force-activated binding suggests that the actin-binding interface of α-catenin has been evolutionarily optimized to sense contractile forces generated by myosin motors (Finer et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data, supported by a citation about myosin force generation.

claim: Force-activated binding enables the cadherin-catenin complex to recognize and preferentially engage pre-stressed actomyosin cables adjacent to the plasma membrane at adherens junctions.
source: We speculate force-activated binding enables the cadherin-catenin complex to recognize and preferentially engage pre-stressed actomyosin cables adjacent to the plasma membrane at adherens junctions (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological function.

claim: Force-activated binding provides a mechanism for initial engagement between actin and the cadherin-associated population of α-catenin, as well as rapidly strengthening adhesion after preliminary attachments are formed.

evidence: This is a speculation about the biological function.

claim: Force-activated binding could facilitate the transition from nascent cell-cell contacts to mature adherens junctions, as punctate nascent adhesions associated with radial actin cables coalesce and spread along a developing circumferential band of tensed actomyosin bundles.
source: This could facilitate the transition from nascent cell-cell contacts to mature adherens junctions, as punctate nascent adhesions associated with radial actin cables coalesce and spread along a developing circumferential band of tensed actomyosin bundles (Vaezi et al., 2002)

evidence: This is a speculation about the biological function, supported by a citation to prior literature.

source: It also provides a mechanism for concentrating the soluble, cytoplasmic α-catenin population at sites of cytoskeletal tension (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological function.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated the cytoplasmic α-catenin population is enriched on actomyosin bundles linked to adherens junctions, where it suppresses lamellipodium activity and promotes adhesion maturation.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated this population is enriched on actomyosin bundles linked to adherens junctions, where it suppresses lamellipodium activity and promotes adhesion maturation (Drees et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Enrichment of cytoplasmic α-catenin has been speculated to occur via local release from the cadherin complex, but this model is difficult to reconcile with its low cellular concentration and the high concentration of soluble α-catenin required to inhibit Arp2/3-mediated actin branching in vitro.
source: While enrichment has been speculated to occur via local release from the cadherin complex, this model is difficult to reconcile with its low cellular concentration and the high concentration of soluble α-catenin required to inhibit Arp2/3-mediated actin branching in vitro (Drees et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a critique of a prior model, supported by a citation.

source: Force-activated binding provides a feasible cellular mechanism for this enrichment of the homodimeric cytoplasmic α-catenin population, driven by enhanced affinity for tensed F-actin rather than mass action effects due to local concentration.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Identification of a functionally separable force-detector in α-catenin with amino-acid level precision will facilitate a detailed examination of proposed models in cell lines and in vivo.
source: Our identification of a functionally separable force-detector in α-catenin with amino-acid level precision will facilitate a detailed examination of these models in cell lines and in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for future research.

claim: Force-activated binding is an additional, rather than alternative, mechanism to catch-bond formation for mechanical regulation of F-actin binding.
source: We note that force-activated binding is an additional, rather than alternative, mechanism to catch-bond formation (Buckley et al., 2014) for mechanical regulation of F-actin binding.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between different mechanistic modes, supported by a citation.

claim: Vinculin lacks force-activated actin-binding activity despite forming catch-bonds with F-actin, strongly suggesting that these two modes of mechanical regulation operate by unique structural mechanisms, likely to fulfill distinct biological functions.
source: Our finding that vinculin lacks this activity despite forming catch-bonds with F-actin (Huang et al., 2017) strongly suggests that these two modes of mechanical regulation operate by unique structural mechanisms, likely to fulfill distinct biological functions.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data and prior literature.

claim: Vinculin's lack of force-activated actin-binding activity is consistent with the ordered sequence of mechanically-regulated binding events underlying its coordination with α-catenin at adherens junctions, where only after preliminary attachments form through the cadherin complex and come under load is vinculin recruited and activated to bind F-actin.
source: Vinculin's lack of force-activated actin-binding activity is consistent with the ordered sequence of mechanically-regulated binding events underlying its coordination with α-catenin at adherens junctions, where only after preliminary attachments form through the cadherin complex and come under load is vinculin recruited and activated to bind F-actin (Yonemura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to prior literature on vinculin recruitment.

claim: The lower force threshold for force-activated binding than catch-bond formation (~1 pN vs. ~10 pN) supports a model in which the formation of initial attachments to the cytoskeleton through the cadherin complex is stimulated through force-activated binding, which is subsequently strengthened by catch-bonding through both α-catenin and vinculin during adhesion maturation.
source: The lower force threshold for force-activated binding than catch-bond formation (~1 pN vs. ~10 pN) supports a model in which the formation of initial attachments to the cytoskeleton through the cadherin complex is stimulated through force-activated binding, which is subsequently strengthened by catch-bonding through both α-catenin and vinculin during adhesion maturation.

source: We believe dissecting the interplay between force-activated binding and catch-bond formation in vitro and in vivo, as well as the structural basis for coordinated actin catch-bonding by α-catenin and vinculin, are important subjects for future studies.
